corrected_value.title: Comparing implicit gender stereotypes between women and men with the Implicit Relational Assessment Procedure.

expert_opinion.quote: The present study systematically replicated the procedures of Drake et al. (2018) and employed the IRAP to assess general gender stereotypes among Japanese university students, who live in a society where gender inequality remains a pressing issue. In the IRAP procedure, participants responded to pairings of binary gender labels (female and male) and trait descriptors (feminine and masculine) by selecting “true” or “false” under instructions emphasizing rapid responding. Participants exhibited response patterns that were primarily pro-congruent with gender stereotypes, reflected in a consistent tendency to affirm matched gender label–trait pairings (i.e., female–feminine and male–masculine). No significant gender differences were found. Nevertheless, we discussed the possibility of stronger stereotype-consistent responses among male participants in pairings involving male labels, as implied by the current data. Correlational analyses were also conducted between the IRAP performances and scores on an explicit measure of egalitarian attitudes, although no clear correlations were found in the majority of analyses. Overall, the results generally replicated those of Drake et al. (2018), demonstrating stereotype-consistent responses in a Japanese sample.

expert_opinion.quote: In their paper of 2011 titled Gender and Philosophical Intuition Wesley Buckwalter and Stephen Stich argue that the intuitions of women and men differ significantly on various types of philosophical questions. Furthermore, men’s intuitions, so the authors, are more in line with traditionally accepted solutions of classical problems.
